source.publisher: National Council for Law Reporting (Kenya Law)
source.verificationMethod: Section anchors resolved and operative text extracted from the Kenya Law Akoma Ntoso edition, then independently cross-checked word-for-word against the gazetted PDF text (37pp) published by the Kenya Trade Network Agency. All 22 excerpts below are verbatim quotations, machine-diffed against that text; every section link was confirmed to resolve to the provision it cites.

relatedInstruments.title: Data Protection (General) Regulations, 2021
relatedInstruments.citation: Legal Notice No. 263 of 2021 — in force 14 Feb 2022
relatedInstruments.relevance: Part V (regs 27–29) sets out the elements of data protection by design or by default; Part VIII (regs 49–50) prescribes when a DPIA is required and how it is conducted. Operationalises ss.31 and 41, and so bears on O3, O4 and F1.

relatedInstruments.title: Data Protection (Registration of Data Controllers and Data Processors) Regulations, 2021
relatedInstruments.relevance: Gives effect to the Part III registration regime, supporting the accountability limb of F4.

relatedInstruments.title: Office of the Data Protection Commissioner — laws, regulations and guidance
relatedInstruments.relevance: Source for subsidiary legislation, sector guidance notes and published enforcement determinations — the record of how these provisions are applied in practice.

criteria.addressed: The Act contains an explicit provision, in operative language, that speaks directly to the safeguard objective.
criteria.partial: A related provision exists, but coverage is incomplete, indirect, or not explicit — the Act addresses part of the objective, reaches it only by implication, or leaves a material gap.
criteria.not_addressed: No relevant provision was identified in the Act, or the safeguard falls outside what a data-protection statute regulates.

methodology.promptTemplate: For Kenya's Data Protection Act, 2019 (Act No. 24 of 2019), assess UN DPI Safeguards Framework principle '{principleName}' ({principleCode}): {principleDescription}. Identify the section(s) of the Act, if any, that address this principle explicitly or by implication. Classify as Addressed / Partial-indirect / Not addressed using the stated criteria. Quote the operative statutory language verbatim and cite the exact section. State whether the principle falls within the scope of a data-protection statute at all.
methodology.scopeNote: Ratings are based on the Data Protection Act, 2019 alone. The Constitution of Kenya (notably Article 27 on equality and Article 31 on privacy), sectoral statutes, and the subsidiary Regulations made under s.71 did not influence any rating — the Regulations are listed under Source text as context for how the Act is applied, not as a basis for scoring. A safeguard scored 'not addressed' is therefore a finding about this Act, not about Kenyan law as a whole.
methodology.reviewStatusLabel: All 22 statutory citations are verified verbatim against the gazetted text and every section link resolves. What awaits review is the analysis: whether each provision amounts to Addressed, Partial or Not addressed is an interpretive judgment, and a reviewer could reasonably disagree.
methodology.preparedBy: Upanzi Network — automated statutory analysis with manual citation verification
methodology.reviewerRole: Policy or legal reviewer (Topi's team / qualified counsel)
methodology.reviewScope: Reviewers are asked to check the Addressed / Partial / Not addressed classifications and the mapping reasoning — not the citations, which are already machine-verified against the primary text. The judgments most open to challenge are flagged per finding.

principles.rationale: The Act supplies exactly what this principle asks for: an explicit legal basis established before processing, plus a standing institution to administer it. Section 3 states the Act's object as establishing 'the legal and institutional mechanism to protect personal data'; section 5 constitutes the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner as a body corporate. The mapping is direct and requires no inference.

evidence.heading: Object and purpose of this Act
evidence.excerpt: The object and purpose of this Act is— (a) to regulate the processing of personal data; (b) to ensure that the processing of personal data of a data subject is guided by the principles set out in section 25; (c) to protect the privacy of individuals; (d) to establish the legal and institutional mechanism to protect personal data; and (e) to provide data subjects with rights and remedies to protect their personal data from processing that is not in accordance with this Act.

evidence.heading: Establishment of the Office
evidence.excerpt: There is established the office of the Data Protection Commissioner which shall be a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal.

principles.mappingExplanation: A dedicated statute with a named regulator means DPI-relevant processing operates under a pre-existing legal basis rather than in a regulatory vacuum. Section 3(d)'s 'legal and institutional mechanism' language maps almost one-to-one onto the principle's requirement that regulatory aspects be embedded from the outset.
principles.limitations: The Act establishes the legal basis for data processing generally. It does not itself authorise any particular DPI system — that authority would come from the sectoral statute governing that system.

principles.rationale: Section 25 codifies purpose limitation, data minimisation and storage limitation as binding obligations, and section 41 imposes a distinct, standing duty of data protection by design and by default that attaches both when the means of processing are determined and when processing occurs.

evidence.heading: Principles of data protection
evidence.excerpt: Every data controller or data processor shall ensure that personal data is— … (c) collected for explicit, specified and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes; (d) adequate, relevant, limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which it is processed; … (g) kept in a form which identifies the data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes which it was collected.

evidence.heading: Data protection by design or by default
evidence.excerpt: Every data controller or data processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures which are designed— (a) to implement the data protection principles in an effective manner; and (b) to integrate necessary safeguards for that purpose into the processing. (2) The duty under subsection (1) applies both at the time of the determination of the means of processing the data and at the time of the processing. (3) A data controller or data processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which is necessary for each specific purpose is processed.

principles.mappingExplanation: Section 41(2) is the operative link to this principle: the duty attaches at the design stage, not merely at runtime, which is precisely what 'privacy by design' requires of DPI architecture. Section 41(3)'s default-minimisation rule and section 25(d) together supply the data-minimisation limb.
principles.limitations: The Act does not use the DPI framework's vocabulary of 'delinking' or 'limiting observability'. Those are architectural properties that s.41 would reach only through the general duty to integrate safeguards, not by name.

principles.rationale: Section 41(4) enumerates the security measures a controller must consider, and names pseudonymisation and encryption expressly — the two techniques this principle calls for — alongside risk identification, safeguards, and restoration of availability.

evidence.heading: Data protection by design or by default
evidence.excerpt: To give effect to this section, the data controller or data processor shall consider measures such as— (a) to identify reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to personal data under the person's possession or control; (b) to establish and maintain appropriate safeguards against the identified risks; (c) to the pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data; (d) to the ability to restore the availability and access to personal data in a timely manner in the event of a physical or technical incident.

principles.mappingExplanation: This is an unusually exact textual match. The DPI principle asks for encryption and pseudonymisation to be incorporated and for legal frameworks to fill gaps where technical design falls short; s.41(4)(c) names both techniques, and s.41(4)(a)–(b) supply the risk-based duty that closes the gap.
principles.limitations: Section 41(4) is framed as measures the controller 'shall consider', which is weaker than an unconditional mandate to deploy encryption in every case.

principles.rationale: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency are binding under section 25(b), and section 30 confines processing to an enumerated set of lawful bases — consent or one of the specified necessity grounds.

evidence.heading: Principles of data protection
evidence.excerpt: Every data controller or data processor shall ensure that personal data is— (a) processed in accordance with the right to privacy of the data subject; (b) processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to any data subject.

evidence.heading: Lawful processing of personal data
evidence.excerpt: A data controller or data processor shall not process personal data, unless— (a) the data subject consents to the processing for one or more specified purposes; or (b) the processing is necessary— (i) for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is a party …

principles.mappingExplanation: Section 30's closed list of lawful bases is the mechanism that keeps processing tied to an authorised purpose, and s.25(a) anchors it to the constitutional right to privacy — together covering the 'lawfully and transparently, within a legal framework' requirement.
principles.limitations: The Act regulates who may process and on what basis; it does not prescribe personnel-level access controls, which s.41's organisational-measures duty would have to carry.

principles.rationale: Section 56 creates a statutory complaints route to the Commissioner with a binding ninety-day conclusion period, and permits oral complaints — a genuine accessibility provision. Section 65 adds an independent civil entitlement to compensation.

evidence.heading: Complaints to the Data Commissioner
evidence.excerpt: A data subject who is aggrieved by a decision of any person under this Act may lodge a complaint with the Data Commissioner in accordance with this Act. (2) A person who intends to lodge a complaint under this Act shall do so orally or in writing. … (5) A complaint made to the Data Commissioner shall be investigated and concluded within ninety days.

evidence.heading: Compensation to a data subject
evidence.excerpt: A person who suffers damage by reason of a contravention of a requirement of this Act is entitled to compensation for that damage from the data controller or the data processor.

principles.mappingExplanation: The principle requires grievance mechanisms accessible to all, equitably. Section 56(2)'s allowance for oral complaints directly addresses the literacy and formality barriers that otherwise make written-only complaint systems exclusionary, and s.56(5)'s time limit converts the right into an enforceable expectation.
principles.limitations: Accessibility beyond the oral/written channel — language, physical access, cost of pursuing a s.65 claim in court — is not addressed by the Act.

principles.rationale: Section 26 confers the core control rights (information, access, objection, correction, deletion), section 32 makes consent withdrawable at any time with the burden of proof on the controller, and section 35 confers a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or significant effects.

evidence.heading: Rights of a data subject
evidence.excerpt: A data subject has a right— (a) to be informed of the use to which their personal data is to be put; (b) to access their personal data in custody of data controller or data processor; (c) to object to the processing of all or part of their personal data; (d) to correction of false or misleading data; and (e) to deletion of false or misleading data about them.

evidence.heading: Automated individual decision making
evidence.excerpt: Every data subject has a right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning or significantly affects the data subject.

evidence.heading: Conditions of consent
evidence.excerpt: A data controller or data processor shall bear the burden of proof for establishing a data subject's consent to the processing of their personal data for a specified purpose. (2) Unless otherwise provided under this Act, a data subject shall have the right to withdraw consent at any time.

principles.mappingExplanation: Section 35 is the provision that matters most for DPI: where eligibility or entitlement is determined algorithmically, it preserves a right to human involvement, which is the substance of agency in an automated service. Section 32(2) makes consent revocable rather than a one-time gate.
principles.limitations: Section 26 grants correction and deletion only for data that is 'false or misleading' — narrower than a general right to erasure, so a data subject cannot demand deletion of accurate data under this section.

principles.partialityReason: The Act delivers institutional accountability — an enforcement body, oversight powers, public-awareness duties — but is silent on the governance-design limb of this principle: democratic participation in DPI design, fair market competition, and vendor lock-in have no counterpart in the statute.
principles.rationale: Section 8 gives the Office a broad oversight, inspection, assessment and public-education mandate, which covers accountability. But the principle also asks for democratic participation and competitive, non-locked-in procurement, and the Act contains nothing on those. Coverage is therefore substantial on one limb and absent on the other.

evidence.heading: Functions of the Office
evidence.excerpt: The Office shall— (a) oversee the implementation of and be responsible for the enforcement of this Act; … (c) exercise oversight on data processing operations, either of own motion or at the request of a data subject, and verify whether the processing of data is done in accordance with this Act; … (f) receive and investigate any complaint by any person on infringements of the rights under this Act; (g) take such measures as may be necessary to bring the provisions of this Act to the knowledge of the general public; (h) carry out inspections of public and private entities with a view to evaluating the processing of personal data.

principles.mappingExplanation: Section 8(1)(c) supports transparency of DPI operations because the Commissioner may act on its own motion — oversight does not depend on someone first filing a complaint. Section 8(1)(g)'s public-awareness duty is the closest the Act comes to the participation limb, but awareness-raising is not participation in design.
principles.limitations: Nothing in the Act addresses procurement, vendor lock-in, open standards, or public consultation on DPI design. Section 71 empowers the Cabinet Secretary to make regulations but attaches no statutory consultation requirement — public participation on the 2021 Regulations happened as a matter of practice and constitutional requirement, not because this Act compels it.

principles.partialityReason: Section 31 mandates a genuine prior risk assessment covering 'risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects', which is substantial coverage. But it is triggered only by high-risk processing, is scoped to data-processing harms, and does not reach non-data harms across a DPI life cycle — exclusion, service denial, or downstream effects on people who are not data subjects.
principles.rationale: This is stronger than a generic mapping: the Act imposes a mandatory, prior, documented impact assessment with a duty to consult the Commissioner where residual risk remains high. The gap is one of scope rather than of kind — the assessment is about processing operations, not about the DPI system as a whole.

evidence.heading: Data protection impact assessment
evidence.excerpt: Where a processing operation is likely to result in high risk to the rights and freedoms of a data subject, by virtue of its nature, scope, context and purposes, a data controller or data processor shall, prior to the processing, carry out a data protection impact assessment. (2) A data protection impact assessment shall include the following— … (c) an assessment of the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects; (d) the measures envisaged to address the risks and the safeguards, security measures and mechanisms to ensure the protection of personal data.

evidence.heading: Principles of data protection
evidence.excerpt: Every data controller or data processor shall ensure that personal data is— (a) processed in accordance with the right to privacy of the data subject.

principles.mappingExplanation: Section 31 is a true anticipate-assess-mitigate provision: it is prospective ('prior to the processing'), explicitly rights-framed, and requires mitigation measures, not just documentation. That is the operative core of 'do no harm'. What it does not do is extend to the full DPI life cycle or to harms that are not mediated by personal-data processing.
principles.limitations: The duty is conditional on a high-risk threshold, so ordinary processing attracts no assessment. Harms to non-data-subjects, and harms arising from a DPI system's design rather than its data processing, fall outside s.31.

principles.partialityReason: The Act protects the characteristics on which discrimination typically turns — race, sex, pregnancy, health status, ethnic origin, age, disability, belief, sexual orientation — but protects them as data categories requiring heightened processing conditions, not as grounds on which unequal treatment or unequal access is prohibited.
principles.rationale: A full-text search of the Act returns zero occurrences of 'discrimination', 'gender' or 'equality'. The Act nonetheless engages the subject matter substantively: s.2 defines sensitive personal data by reference to protected characteristics, Part V restricts its processing, and s.35 constrains profiling. This is meaningful but oblique coverage — it regulates the handling of identity data rather than guaranteeing equal treatment.

evidence.heading: Interpretation — "sensitive personal data"
evidence.excerpt: "sensitive personal data" means data revealing the natural person's race, health status, ethnic social origin, conscience, belief, genetic data, biometric data, property details, marital status, family details including names of the person's children, parents, spouse or spouses, sex or the sexual orientation of the data subject.

evidence.heading: Processing of sensitive personal data
evidence.excerpt: No category of sensitive personal data shall be processed unless section 25 applies to that processing.

evidence.heading: Permitted grounds for processing sensitive personal data
evidence.excerpt: Without prejudice to section 44, sensitive personal data of a data subject may be processed where— (a) the processing is carried out in the course of legitimate activities with appropriate safeguards by a foundation, association or any other not-for profit body with a political, philosophical, religious or trade union aim…

evidence.heading: Automated individual decision making
evidence.excerpt: Every data subject has a right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning or significantly affects the data subject.

principles.mappingExplanation: The route from these provisions to 'do not discriminate' runs through profiling: s.35 limits automated decisions, and Part V raises the bar for processing precisely the attributes that discriminatory profiling would rely on. Together they constrain the mechanism of algorithmic discrimination without ever prohibiting discrimination as such.
principles.limitations: Equality and non-discrimination are guaranteed by Article 27 of the Constitution of Kenya, which is outside the scope of this analysis. A finding of 'partial' here reflects the Act's silence, not the absence of protection in Kenyan law.

principles.outOfScopeNote: This principle is chiefly about DPI service design — accessible interfaces, channel choice, outreach to structurally excluded groups. A data-protection statute governs how personal data is handled, not how a service is delivered. Kenya's protections on this front would live in disability, gender and sectoral service legislation, not here.
principles.partialityReason: The Act reaches age and disability, but only in specific procedural respects: heightened protection for children's data, and a mechanism for exercising rights through a guardian where the data subject has a disability. Gender appears only as a protected data category, never as a design consideration.
principles.rationale: Two provisions engage this principle directly. Section 33 imposes child-specific consent and best-interests duties with an explicit harm test. Section 27(b) provides for rights to be exercised on behalf of a data subject with a mental or other disability. Neither addresses whether a DPI system's design creates barriers for these groups.

evidence.heading: Processing of personal data relating to a child
evidence.excerpt: Every data controller or data processor shall not process personal data relating to a child unless— (a) consent is given by the child's parent or guardian; and (b) the processing is in such a manner that protects and advances the rights and best interests of the child. … (3) Mechanisms contemplated under sub-section (2) shall be determined on the basis of— … (d) possibility of harm to a child arising out of processing of personal data.

evidence.heading: Exercise of rights of data subjects
evidence.excerpt: A right conferred on a data subject may be exercised— (a) where the data subject is a minor, by a person who has parental authority or by a guardian; (b) where the data subject has a mental or other disability, by a person duly authorised to act as their guardian or administrator.

principles.mappingExplanation: Section 27(b) is the Act's only substantive engagement with disability, and it is an accommodation for exercising rights rather than a duty to design accessibly. Section 33 is a genuine age-responsive protection. Neither speaks to gender, and none addresses barriers to access — which is where this principle's weight actually sits.
principles.limitations: Scoring this 'partial' rather than 'not addressed' credits the age and disability provisions that do exist. Reading the result as a verdict on Kenya's overall responsiveness to gender, ability and age would be a category error — the relevant law is elsewhere.

principles.outOfScopeNote: 'Do not exclude' turns on whether a service offers non-digital channels and refrains from making digital enrolment mandatory. That is a service-delivery mandate, not a data-processing rule. It belongs in the statute establishing the particular DPI system — the national ID, e-government or social-protection legislation — not in a data-protection Act.
principles.rationale: No provision of the Act addresses channel choice, mandatory digital enrolment, or non-digital alternatives. Section 4 does contemplate non-automated processing, but only to define the Act's own application; it imposes no duty on any service to offer an offline route.

nearestProvision.heading: Application
nearestProvision.excerpt: This Act applies to the processing of personal data— (a) entered in a record, by or for a data controller or processor, by making use of automated or non-automated means: Provided that when the recorded personal data is processed by non-automated means, it forms a whole or part of a filing system.
nearestProvision.whyInsufficient: This is a scoping clause that extends the Act's reach to paper records. It says nothing about whether a data subject is entitled to a non-digital channel, which is what the principle requires.

principles.mappingExplanation: No provision found. The Act regulates the processing of personal data once collected; it does not reach the anterior question of which access channels a public service must offer, or whether digital enrolment may be made a condition of access.
principles.limitations: This is a finding about the Data Protection Act, 2019 in isolation. Kenya's obligations on service accessibility arise under other instruments and were not examined.
